papers.metric: likelihood of first approval (%) phase 1 to FDA approval
papers.value_source_sentence: Our study reveals an average likelihood of first approval rate of 14.3% across leading research-based pharmaceutical companies, broadly ranging from 8% to 23%.

papers.metric: clinical approval success rate (%) self-originated, top 10 firms
papers.value_source_sentence: For self-originated compounds, the clinical approval success rates were 14.3%, 16.4%, and 18.4% for top 10 firms, top 11-20 firms, and top 21-50 firms, respectively.

papers.metric: probability of FDA approval (%) from testing entry
papers.value_source_sentence: The probability of a drug completing all phases of testing and obtaining FDA approval was 7%, which is below the 11% industry average.

papers.metric: overall FDA approval rate (%)
papers.value_source_sentence: A total of 40 agents reached FDA approval, with an overall approval rate of 6.1%.

papers.metric: % of phase 1 trials leading to registered pediatric drug
papers.value_source_sentence: Seven trials (5%) led to drugs being registered for pediatric use in therapy of cancer.

caveats: Endpoints differ slightly: 'likelihood of first approval' and 'clinical approval success rate' (industry-wide, phase 1 to approval) vs oncology-specific FDA approval/registration rates. Denominators differ (active ingredients, firms, distinct agents, phase 1 trials). Comparable only as order-of-magnitude estimates of translational success.

papers.metric: estimated non-publication rate (%)
papers.value_source_sentence: We estimate that a further 214 experiments (in addition to the 1,359 identified through rigorous systematic review; non publication rate 14%) have been conducted but not reported.

papers.metric: estimated % experiments published (researcher opinion)
papers.value_source_sentence: On average, those working in not-for-profit institutes (n = 421) estimated that 50 percent (interquartile range (IQR) 35 to 70) of all conducted laboratory animal experiments are published.

papers.metric: % animal-study proposals published
papers.value_source_sentence: Results showed that the publication rate increased from 67% in our follow-up study to 70%.

papers.metric: % drugs with no efficacy studies published before first trial
papers.value_source_sentence: Most (87%) accessible animal efficacy studies were reported after publication of the first trial, and for 17% of the drugs in our sample, no efficacy studies were published before the first trial report.

caveats: Metrics are not identical: missing-experiment estimate (Sena), opinion of % published (ter Riet), empirical publication rate (Deutsch), drug-cohort pre-trial publication (Federico). Comparable only as bounds on non-publication.

papers.metric: human-mouse concordance (R^2)
papers.value_source_sentence: Among genes changed significantly in humans, the murine orthologs are close to random in matching their human counterparts (e.g., R(2) between 0.0 and 0.1).

papers.metric: human-mouse concordance (Spearman rho)
papers.value_source_sentence: Contrary to the previous findings, the gene expression levels in the mouse models showed extraordinarily significant correlations with those of the human conditions (Spearman's rank correlation coefficient: 0.43-0.68; genes changed in the same direction: 77-93%; P = 6.5 × 10(-11) to 1.2 × 10(-35)).

caveats: Correlation metrics differ (R^2 vs Spearman rho) and are not directly numerically comparable; the point is the qualitative reversal from the same underlying data.

papers.metric: effect-size inflation from unblinded ischemia induction
papers.value_source_sentence: Studies that included unblinded induction of ischemia reported effect sizes 13.1% (95% CI, 26.4% to 0.2%) greater than studies that included blinding, and studies that included healthy animals instead of animals with comorbidities overstated the effect size by 11.5% (95% CI, 21.2% to 1.8%).

papers.metric: effect-size inflation from lack of blinded assessment
papers.value_source_sentence: More than half of the studies (51.2%) did not report blinded assessment, constituting a likely source of evaluation bias, with an overstated effect size of 7.2%.

papers.metric: efficacy overestimation from publication bias
papers.value_source_sentence: Inclusion of these theoretical missing studies suggested a 27% overestimation of efficacy, reducing the overall efficacy to a 15% improvement in locomotor recovery.

caveats: Metrics differ: two report percentage-point effect-size inflation from a single design item (blinding), one reports proportional efficacy overestimation from publication-bias correction.
Disease areas differ (stroke vs SCI).
Denominators are animals pooled across differing numbers of meta-analyses/studies.

papers.metric: publications reporting a sample-size calculation
papers.value_source_sentence: A sample-size calculation was rarely used (four (5%) of 77).

papers.metric: DRF experiments presenting a power/sample-size calculation
papers.value_source_sentence: Even though all the experiments were reported as approved by animal research review committees, such as an Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee, which typically require justification for animal numbers in an experiment, no power or sample size calculation was presented for any of the 28 DRF experiments.
papers.experimental_conditions: literature review of DRF studies 2000-2013 plus updates

papers.metric: studies not reporting analgesia use
papers.value_source_sentence: Thirteen percent of studies (n = 27) failed to report use of anaesthesia and 97% (n = 206) did not report analgesia use.

caveats: Different metrics (sample-size calc vs analgesia reporting) and different fields (critical care, radiation countermeasures, six intervention areas); all are reporting-compliance percentages but not the same denominator or the same 3R.

papers.metric: reduction in DRF experiment sample size via power calculation
papers.value: less than half of typical numbers
papers.value_source_sentence: Even so, our calculated samples sizes were less than half of the original and typically used sample size for a DRF experiment.

papers.metric: reduction in mice per experiment via refined pulmonary-embolism model
papers.value_source_sentence: Not only were they successful in strengthening the model by broadening the spectrum beyond a single extreme (i.e. fatal pulmonary embolism) and measuring a specific biological response rather than events with non-specific causes, but also they were able to reduce the number of mice per experiment by around 90% ().

papers.metric: reduction in current control animals via historical controls
papers.value_source_sentence: We show that, under our simulation conditions, the number of current control subjects can be reduced by more than half by including historical controls in the analyses.

caveats: Reductions are relative to different baselines (whole experiment vs control group only) and via different mechanisms; percentages are not directly additive.

papers.metric: Reusability sub-score (of 10)
papers.value_source_sentence: The average for each metric was as follows: findability, 3.4 (2.7) of 7; accessibility, 1.0 (1.0) of 3; interoperability, 1.1 (1.2) of 4; and reusability, 2.4 (2.6) of 10.

papers.metric: Reusable score (of 10)
papers.value_source_sentence: The FAIR assessments revealed moderate to low levels of compliance across datasets, with Reusable scores ranging from 2 to 3 out of 10, and Interoperability often being the weakest dimension.
papers.experimental_conditions: Publicly available datasets from international agencies
papers.method: F-UJI automated assessment tool (17 FAIR metrics)

caveats: Different assessment tools: custom Wilkinson v0.3d specification (dental) vs F-UJI (air quality).
Different units of assessment: individual articles that shared data (n=112) vs whole datasets (n=4).
Air quality value is a reported range (2-3), dental is a mean with SD.

papers.metric: % of DMSPs addressing all six required elements
papers.value_source_sentence: We evaluated the content of the 358 DMSPs using the rubric developed for this study (Supplementary Material); 79.3% of them addressed all six required elements outlined in the NIH DMS Policy.

papers.metric: % of DMP projects with data-sharing score 0
papers.value_source_sentence: Of the 25 projects for which we attempted to locate shared datasets and generate a DATA score, nineteen (76%) had an overall score of 0 ( Fig 1 ).

papers.metric: % actual public data availability
papers.value_source_sentence: Meta-analyses showed a prevalence of declared and actual public data availability of 8% (95% confidence interval 5% to 11%) and 2% (1% to 3%), respectively, between 2016 and 2021.
papers.n_definition: original research articles in meta-research studies

caveats: Metrics measure different constructs: % of plans that are complete (DMSP), % of projects scoring zero on a sharing rubric (NSF), and % of articles with actually-available public data (BMJ meta-analysis).
Polarity differs: the DMSP value is a positive completeness rate; the NSF (76%) and the availability gap are non-sharing/low-sharing measures.
Units differ: plans (358), projects (25), articles (2,121,580).
BMJ value is a pooled meta-analytic estimate with a CI; the others are single-study point estimates.

papers.metric: % of medical papers that actually shared data publicly (2016-2021)
papers.value_source_sentence: Aggregation of the findings of sufficiently similar studies suggested that on average, 8% of medical papers published between 2016 and 2021 declared that their data were publicly available and 2% actually shared their data publicly.

papers.metric: % of articles whose raw data were easily available on request
papers.value_source_sentence: The percentage of data easily available from the 157 articles was only 4.5% (95% CI 1.8% to 9%).
papers.experimental_conditions: data requested by email / checked availability

papers.metric: % of authors promising data who actually provided it on request
papers.value_source_sentence: Among 254 (14%) of 1792 authors who responded to our query for data sharing, only 123 (6.8%) provided the requested data.
papers.scope_population: articles with data-availability statement promising sharing

papers.metric: % of declared-available datasets meeting key FAIR criteria
papers.value_source_sentence: Furthermore, when data were available for assessment, only one study (0.3%, 95% CI: 0–2%) was found to comply with the remaining four FAIR assessment criteria (Fig.).
papers.experimental_conditions: declared availability checked against FAIR self-assessment

caveats: Metric definitions differ: 'actually shared publicly' vs 'easily available on request' vs 'provided data when emailed' vs 'FAIR-compliant among those declared available' - all capture 'reader can actually get usable data' but are not identical.
Denominators differ (all sampled articles vs only those with a share-promising statement).
Scope ranges from whole-literature meta-analysis to single-journal audits.

papers.metric: potential reduction in animal use from replacing control animals with VCGs
papers.value_source_sentence: The use of VCGs has the potential of a 25% reduction in animal use by replacing the control group animals with existing randomized data sets.
papers.experimental_conditions: proposal; full replacement of concurrent control animals

papers.metric: reduction in concurrent control animals from HCD-derived VCGs
papers.value_source_sentence: Virtual control groups (VCGs) created from historical control data (HCD) can reduce the number of concurrent control group animals needed in regulatory toxicity studies by up to 25%.

papers.metric: potential reduction of animal use via VCG replacement of concurrent controls
papers.value_source_sentence: Recently, using VCG as a replacement for concurrent controls has been closely evaluated in the preclinical space, considering this might reduce animal use in toxicology studies by up to 25%.

papers.metric: reduction in enrolled patients under congruent Bayesian dynamic borrowing (device trial)
papers.value_source_sentence: The proposed design, when evaluated under scenarios where historical and current data were congruent (scenarios 1 and 2), demonstrated a significant reduction in the number of enrolled patients (1,497 vs. 2,386 under H​ and 1,850 vs. 2,386 under H​) while maintaining both the T1E and Power at their nominal levels.
papers.experimental_conditions: congruent historical controls; group-sequential SAM prior

caveats: First three entries are preclinical animal-reduction estimates (% of control animals); the fourth is a clinical-trial patient-enrollment reduction and is not directly comparable in units or population.
altex.2001311, altex.2403141 and 01926233241300310 report the same 25% figure but two cite the concept paper, so they are not fully independent estimates.
Device-trial value is a raw count (1,497 vs 2,386), not a percentage; approx 37% enrollment reduction.

papers.metric: % of significant parameters confirmed after omitting the concurrent control group (NHP)
papers.value_source_sentence: Our investigation has demonstrated that out of 22 parameters with statistical difference in the fixed-effect ANOVA /Dunnett’s test, 82% could be confirmed using the mixed-design ANOVA.
papers.experimental_conditions: concurrent control omitted; mixed-design ANOVA vs fixed-effect ANOVA/Dunnett

papers.metric: % of pairwise comparisons with >=90% effect-size agreement between CCG and VCG (rat)
papers.value_source_sentence: In 68.5% of all the pairwise comparisons performed there was at least 90% agreement in effect size estimate between analysis done with CCG and VCGs.
papers.experimental_conditions: VCG vs concurrent control; liver enzymes

papers.metric: % of quantitative parameters NON-reproducible when CCG replaced by VCG (rat, worst legacy study)
papers.value_source_sentence: When the CCG was replaced with VCG, the result showed that 31% (34 of 108 parameters), 40% (43 out of 107 parameters), and 49% (57 of 115 parameters) of the quantitative parameters were not statistically reproducible in the legacy studies A, B and C respectively ().

caveats: Metrics are not identical: parameter-confirmation (NHP), >=90% effect-size agreement (rat), and non-reproducibility rate (rat) measure related but distinct quantities.
Species differ (NHP vs rat); the 49% entry is a non-reproducibility rate (higher = worse), the opposite polarity to the agreement/confirmation percentages.
10.1177/01926233241300310 and 10.3389/fphar.2026.1704002 are already in the prior evidence set; reused here only as figure comparators.

papers.metric: animals in shared historical control tumour database (RITA)
papers.value_source_sentence: In the RITA database, there are currently 10,896 rats from 106 studies with more than 17,604 primary tumors and 16,551 pre-neoplastic lesions.

papers.metric: control/toxicology animals analysed in eTRANSAFE
papers.value_source_sentence: The opportunities and challenges for implementing VCGs were the focus of the IMI eTRANSAFE project, which has collected and analyzed drug safety and toxicology data from more than 60,000 rats, 1,300 dogs and 500 monkeys (see ref.and more recently ref.).

papers.metric: legacy studies integrated from eTOX into eTRANSAFE
papers.value_source_sentence: Further in vivo animal toxicology study data have been made available through the integration of 6500 preclinical studies from the eTOX project [] into the eTRANSAFE ToxHub System.

papers.metric: SEND-format studies in FDA CDER repository queried
papers.value_source_sentence: FDA CDER's repository of >1800 sponsor-submitted studies in SEND format was queried using the statistical programming language R to gain insight into how the CDISC SEND Implementation Guides are being applied across the industry.

papers.metric: SEND datasets in FDA CDER repository (later count)
papers.value_source_sentence: The US FDA CDER repository having more than 10,000 sponsor-submitted SEND datasets provides the opportunity for large-scale, cross-data analysis of toxicology data, which can ultimately provide safer compounds to patients faster.

caveats: Units differ across entries: animals (RITA 10,896 rats; eTRANSAFE 60,000 rats/1,300 dogs/500 monkeys) vs studies (eTOX 6,500; CDER >1,800) vs datasets (CDER >10,000) - not directly comparable on one axis.
The two FDA CDER SEND counts (>1,800 in 2020 and >10,000 in 2024) are the same repository at different times, showing growth rather than independent resources.
n encodes the primary count per entry (animals or studies/datasets) as noted in n_definition.

papers.metric: overall accuracy (Derek Nexus vs reference)
papers.value_source_sentence: Derek Nexus predicted phototoxicity of the compounds, with a sensitivity of 63%, specificity of 93%, Positive Predictive Values of 90% and Negative Predictive Value of 69%, overall accuracy of 77% and balanced accuracy of 78%.
papers.n_definition: compounds tested (not stated numerically in abstract)
papers.experimental_conditions: expert-rule software (Derek Nexus) vs known phototoxicity outcomes

papers.metric: external-validation accuracy
papers.value_source_sentence: The accuracy (ACC) values of the most successful model were 83.82% for the internal and 94.11% for the external validation.

papers.metric: cross-validation success rate of interspecies models
papers.value_source_sentence: All models had a cross- validation success rates > 75%, with 74% (17 models) of the models having a cross- validation success rates > 80%, indicating that all of models with the high reliability (;).
papers.experimental_conditions: QSAR + interspecies correlation estimation + species sensitivity distribution

caveats: Different endpoints (phototoxicity, pregnancy category, aquatic toxicity)
Different performance metrics (classification accuracy vs cross-validation success rate)
Different reference standards (known in vivo/clinical outcomes vs experimental aquatic toxicity data)
n definitions differ (compounds vs antibiotics vs models)

papers.metric: unique substances in FAIR suspect-list resource
papers.value_source_sentence: The NORMAN-SLE contains 99 separate suspect list collections (as of May 2022) from over 70 contributors around the world, totalling over 100,000 unique substances.
papers.experimental_conditions: 99 curated collections from >70 contributors, DOIs+versioning via Zenodo

papers.metric: nanomaterials in integrated libraries
papers.value_source_sentence: These established and well-characterized NM libraries (e.g. NanoMILE, NanoSolutions, NANoREG, NanoFASE, caLIBRAte, NanoTEST and the Nanomaterial Registry (>2000 NMs)) contain physicochemical characterization data as well as data for several relevant biological endpoints, assessed in part using harmonized Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) methods and test guidelines.
papers.experimental_conditions: aggregated EU NM libraries with OECD-harmonised endpoints

papers.metric: public proteomic datasets meta-analysed
papers.value_source_sentence: As a case study, we performed a meta-analysis of 25 proteomic datasets to investigate the toxicological effects of nanomaterials at the lung level.
papers.experimental_conditions: harmonized meta-analysis per OECD Omics Reporting Framework

caveats: Counts measure fundamentally different entities (chemical substances vs engineered nanomaterials vs public omics datasets)
Different resource types (suspect-list exchange, nanoinformatics library platform, proteomic meta-analysis workflow)
Values span several orders of magnitude and are not additive or directly comparable

papers.metric: sensitivity / specificity vs in vivo genotoxicity
papers.value_source_sentence: The capacity of the assay to predict expected genotoxic effects of a difficult set of coded chemicals was very good, providing a sensitivity of 77 (80)% and a specificity of 88 (97)%.

papers.metric: sensitivity / specificity vs in vivo genotoxicity
papers.value_source_sentence: This trial confirmed the accuracy of ToxTracker to predict in vivo genotoxicants with a sensitivity of 84.4% and a specificity of 91.2%.

papers.metric: sensitivity / specificity vs in vivo skin sensitisation
papers.value_source_sentence: The overall accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity were 76.2% (32/42), 85.0% (17/20), and 68.2% (15/22), respectively, with the predictivity for liquid formulations being slightly higher compared to the solid formulations.

papers.metric: sensitivity / predictivity vs known hepatotoxins
papers.value_source_sentence: Of the 42 selected known hepatotoxins in the set, 36 elicited detectable toxicity effects in the spheroid hepatotoxicity assay (86% sensitivity), whereas all compounds considered “safe” had no effect on the number of live cells or spheroid phenotype (100% predictivity).

papers.metric: balanced accuracy vs literature consensus
papers.value_source_sentence: Balanced accuracies ranged from 0.55 to 0.88 ().

caveats: Reference standards differ: in vivo genotoxicity (geaa009, em.22592), in vivo skin sensitisation (yrtph.2024.105595), known hepatotoxins (adt.2016.729), literature consensus for metabolic disruption (EHP6779).
Metrics are not identical: sensitivity/specificity pairs for four assays vs balanced accuracy range for EHP6779.
Endpoints span different organs/hazards (genotoxicity, sensitisation, hepatotoxicity, metabolic disruption); values should not be pooled as a single accuracy.
EHP6779 value is a model balanced-accuracy range across model variants, not a single-assay sensitivity.

papers.metric: % admitting data fabrication/falsification at least once (self, pooled)
papers.value_source_sentence: Meta-analysis yielded a pooled weighted estimate of 1.97% (95%CI: 0.86–4.45), with significant heterogeneity (Cochran's Q = 61.7777, df = 6, P<0.0001).

papers.metric: % admitting use of at least one QRP
papers.value_source_sentence: Ninety-four per cent admitted that they had used at least one of these QRPs, and the mean self-reported rate across all QRP items was 42%, with rates for the individual QRPs ranging from 17% to 57%.

papers.metric: % implicitly associating QRPs with success
papers.value_source_sentence: Our main finding is that a considerable fraction of about a fifth of researchers associate success with problematic research practices, while only a small minority connect FFP and success.

caveats: Metrics differ: serious FFP admission vs any-QRP admission vs implicit association with success - not directly comparable magnitudes
n definitions differ: pooled survey questions vs individual respondents

papers.metric: % biomedical RPT guidelines mentioning peer-reviewed publication count / data sharing
papers.value_source_sentence: Thirty two (35%) institutions had at least one mention of a specific number of peer reviewed publications.

papers.metric: % research-intensive institutions mentioning the JIF in RPT
papers.value_source_sentence: The percentage was higher for R-type institutions (40%) than for either M-type (18%) or B-type (0%) institutions (Table 2).

caveats: Different metrics (publication-count vs JIF mention) and regions (international vs US/Canada)

papers.metric: % declared vs % actually publicly available (clinical trials)
papers.value_source_sentence: The commitment to data sharing substantially decreases when we consider indicators of actual vs declared data sharing: of 334 articles declaring that they would share data, only 2 IPD sets (0.6%; 95% CI, 0.0%-1.5%) were actually deidentified and publicly available on the journal website.

papers.metric: % articles sharing raw data (psychology)
papers.value_source_sentence: Over half of the articles were publicly available (154/237, 65%, 95% confidence interval [CI] = [59%, 71%]); however, sharing of research materials (26/183; 14%, 95% CI = [10%, 19%]), study protocols (0/188; 0%, 95% CI = [0%, 1%]), raw data (4/188; 2%, 95% CI = [1%, 4%]), and analysis scripts (1/188; 1%, 95% CI = [0%, 1%]) was rare.

papers.metric: % articles with a data-sharing statement (orthopaedics)
papers.value_source_sentence: Of the 1,084 reviewed articles, only 14% included a DSS.

caveats: Metrics differ: declared-vs-actual availability vs raw-data-sharing rate vs data-statement presence
Fields differ (clinical trials vs psychology vs orthopaedics)

papers.metric: papers reporting ethics/3Rs compliance statement (before vs after ARRIVE)
papers.value_source_sentence: This percentage increased to 66% (p = 0.26) after ARRIVE guidelines were published.

papers.metric: papers fully reporting randomization (2009 vs 2019)
papers.value_source_sentence: Full reporting of randomization increased over time from 13.6% to 85.7% [95% confidence interval (CI), 57.8-86.6%; p < 0.0001], as did sample size estimation (from 0% to 20%; 95% CI, 7.6-32.4%; p = 0.002).

papers.metric: articles meeting all Landis 4 bias items (before vs after Nature checklist)
papers.value_source_sentence: The number of NPG articles meeting all relevant Landis 4 criteria increased from 0/203 prior to May 2013 to 31/181 (16.4%) after (two-sample test for equality of proportions without continuity correction, Χ²=36.2, df=1, p=1.8×10).
papers.experimental_conditions: before vs after May 2013 editorial policy

papers.metric: studies with 'poor' reporting quality (Pre-ARRIVE1.0 -> Post-ARRIVE2.0)
papers.value_source_sentence: The rate of studies with "average" reporting quality increased sequentially from 53.95% to 73.94% and then to 90.20%, and those with "poor" reporting quality decreased sequentially from 46.05% to 26.06% and then to 9.55% across the three periods.

papers.metric: manuscripts reporting animal husbandry (control vs ARRIVE-checklist intervention)
papers.value_source_sentence: Details of animal husbandry (ARRIVE subitem 9b) was the only subitem to show improvements in reporting, with the proportion of compliant manuscripts rising from 52.1 to 74.1% ( = 34.0, df = 1, = 2.1 × 10) in the control and intervention groups, respectively.

caveats: Metrics differ: single-item reporting (randomization, husbandry, ethics statement) vs composite (Landis 4) vs reporting-quality band.
'Before/after' contrasts differ: calendar time (2009 vs 2019), pre/post ARRIVE publication, pre/post editorial policy, and RCT control vs intervention.
Denominators differ (single journal vs multi-journal vs mega-journal).
Comparison is illustrative of heterogeneity, not a like-for-like effect-size pooling.

papers.metric: statements indicating data deposited in a repository
papers.value_source_sentence: However, only about 20% of statements indicate that data are deposited in a repository, which the PLOS policy states is the preferred method.

papers.metric: prevalence of declared vs actual public data availability
papers.value_source_sentence: Meta-analyses showed a prevalence of declared and actual public data availability of 8% (95% confidence interval 5% to 11%) and 2% (1% to 3%), respectively, between 2016 and 2021.

papers.metric: declared vs actual vs FAIR-compliant data availability
papers.value_source_sentence: However, when data availability was investigated this percentage dropped to 16% (49/306, 95% CI: 12-20%), and then to less than 1% (1/306, 95% CI: 0-2%) when data were checked for compliance with key FAIR principles.
papers.method: cross-sectional check of statements + FAIR audit

caveats: PLOS ONE metric is repository-deposit share among statements; others are declared/actual public availability across many journals.
Denominator definitions differ (papers vs meta-research studies vs articles).
FAIR-compliance sub-metric available only for the oncology study.

papers.metric: publications sharing all relevant data (2014 vs 2023)
papers.value_source_sentence: The fraction of publications that share all relevant data increased significantly, from 7% in 2014 to 45% in 2023.

papers.metric: actual public data availability (field-wide)
papers.value_source_sentence: Meta-analyses showed a prevalence of declared and actual public data availability of 8% (95% confidence interval 5% to 11%) and 2% (1% to 3%), respectively, between 2016 and 2021.

papers.metric: actual public data availability (oncology)
papers.value_source_sentence: However, when data availability was investigated this percentage dropped to 16% (49/306, 95% CI: 12-20%), and then to less than 1% (1/306, 95% CI: 0-2%) when data were checked for compliance with key FAIR principles.

caveats: Edinburgh entry is single-institution manual scoring of 'all relevant data shared' (incl. supplementary/genomic); the other two are field-wide verified public availability.
Time windows differ (2014-2023 vs 2016-2021 vs 2019).
FAIR-compliance sub-metric available only for the oncology study.
